client: Hey Luna. So, I lost my grandma about six months ago, and ever since then, family gatherings just feel... empty. Everyone else seems to be moving on, laughing and chatting like normal, but I just sit there feeling completely alone in a room full of people. I don't even know if talking about it will help - it's not like it'll bring her back.
therapist:
I hear how deeply you're still grieving your grandma's absence, and how isolating it feels when others seem to have moved on while you're holding this heavy loss. It might be worth exploring - what thoughts come up when you see your family laughing together?  

Would you be open to sharing what you miss most about those family gatherings when your grandma was there?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I miss how she'd always notice when I was quiet in the corner and come sit with me. Now when I see everyone laughing, I just think... shouldn't they be sad too? It makes me feel guilty when I can't join in, like I'm the one who's not moving on properly.
therapist:
Your voice softens when you describe those tender moments with your grandma - it sounds like she had a special way of making you feel seen and cared for.  

When you talk about feeling guilty for not joining in the laughter, I wonder if part of you feels pressured to grieve on the same timeline as others? What would it feel like to let yourself honor your own process?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: It's just... I don't know how to honor my own process when it feels like everyone else has already moved on. Like if I'm still sad, I'm the one being difficult or bringing down the mood. Sometimes I wonder if I'm holding onto the grief too tightly because I'm scared of forgetting her.
therapist:
It sounds like you're carrying two heavy burdens - the grief itself, and this worry about how your grief affects others. That thoughtful pause when you said "I wonder if I'm holding on too tightly" makes me think this is something you've really sat with.  

What comes up when you imagine that honoring your grief could actually be a way of keeping your grandma's memory alive, rather than forgetting her?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: That actually makes me tear up a little. I guess I've been thinking of grief as something negative, like a weight I need to eventually drop. But maybe... maybe carrying her memory this way isn't so bad. Though it still feels lonely when no one else seems to still be carrying it with them.
therapist:
Your voice lights up with a mix of sadness and something like hope as you reconsider what grief might mean - I can hear how meaningful this shift in perspective feels for you.  

That loneliness when others don't seem to share your grief must be so hard - could you tell me more about what you wish others might understand about how you're feeling?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: I wish they'd understand that I'm not trying to be difficult - I just need someone to acknowledge that it's okay if I'm not ready to be all cheerful yet. But when I try to explain that, I just get these awkward silences or quick subject changes, and that makes me feel even more alone. Maybe they think bringing her up will make me sadder, but avoiding her memory hurts more.
therapist:
It sounds like what you're really longing for is simply to be met where you are - not pushed to be cheerful, but not avoided either. That quiet courage in your voice when you say "avoiding her memory hurts more" tells me how much love is woven into your grief.  

Have you noticed any moments when someone has responded in a way that did feel comforting or understanding? Even small gestures?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Actually, my little cousin surprised me last week. She brought me a seashell she found that reminded her of grandma's collection. It was such a small thing, but it meant everything that she wasn't afraid to mention her. Though now I'm worried I made her feel awkward by crying when she gave it to me.
therapist:
What a beautiful moment - your voice lifts when you describe your cousin's thoughtful gesture, even through the tears. That mix of sadness and appreciation you feel seems so natural when someone honors your grandma's memory with you.  

I'm curious - what would it feel like to thank your cousin for that gift, just as she was brave enough to give it to you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I think I'd feel nervous thanking her because I don't want her to think she did something wrong by making me cry. At the same time, it meant so much that she remembered grandma too. Maybe I could tell her how much it meant without making a big emotional scene about it.
therapist:
Your concern for your cousin's feelings comes through so clearly, even as you recognize how meaningful her gesture was. That careful balance you're trying to strike - expressing gratitude while managing emotions - feels very understandable.  

What do you imagine might happen if you let your cousin see just how much her thoughtfulness meant to you, tears and all?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess I'm afraid she'll feel awkward or unsure how to respond, especially since she's younger. But maybe she'd understand better than I think - she did give me the shell, after all. It's just hard to be vulnerable like that when I'm used to hiding how much I'm still hurting.
therapist:
It sounds like you're wrestling with wanting to be open about your feelings while also protecting your cousin from potential discomfort. Your voice quickens as you share this - I can hear how much this means to you.  

What might it feel like to trust that your cousin's kind gesture was her way of saying she wants to support you, even if it's a bit uncertain?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I guess I feel like I've been so focused on not being a burden to others that I haven't considered they might actually want to support me. It's just... what if I open up and it makes things awkward? But then again, keeping everything bottled up hasn't been helping either. It's confusing trying to figure out what's the right way to handle this.
therapist:
Your voice carries a mix of worry and hope as you share this struggle - it sounds like you're starting to see that there might be middle ground between keeping everything bottled up and fearing you'll burden others.  

What would it feel like to start small - maybe sharing just a bit more with someone you trust, like your cousin, and seeing how it goes?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: Starting small sounds... scary, but maybe manageable? I think I could say something simple like "That shell really reminded me of grandma - thank you for thinking of me." Though part of me worries she'll freeze up or not know what to say back. I guess I won't know unless I try, but it's still hard to push past that fear of making things awkward.
therapist:
There's a hopeful energy in your voice as you consider reaching out - I can hear how meaningful this connection could be for you, even through the nervousness.  

What feels different about this small step compared to holding everything in? It seems like part of you is ready to let others show they care, even if it feels uncertain.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech
